faqs.q: Rats are around my Cambridge home near the waterfront — what does control look like?
faqs.a: Near the marinas and seafood blocks, Norway rats live off fish waste and dumpsters and shelter in the crawlspaces and wall voids of the older buildings. Maryland exempts rat control from the Wildlife Damage Control Permit, so be wary of anyone who says a licensed operator is legally required for rats — thoroughness is what you are buying, not a credential. We map the burrows and runs, trap where the sign is, and seal the foundation and utility penetrations rats use to enter, while the food source gets addressed with the property or business owner. Waterfront rat work is a program over several visits, not a single afternoon, and we will lay out that schedule honestly.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Cambridge?
faqs.a: Cambridge jobs sort by neighborhood. A historic-district home with bats in the attic prices around the exclusion: how many entries the old roofline has and whether the colony size triggers the state's approval step for spring and summer work. A waterfront home with raccoons in the crawlspace and rats around the foundation is a different, larger program. Edge properties add groundhog burrows and outbuildings. We inspect the whole property, explain which program each problem belongs to, and give you the full figure for the work you approve before anything starts.

Cambridge.wildlife_intro:
Cambridge is a working Choptank River port and Dorchester County's seat, with a historic district of brick and frame homes, a marina and seafood waterfront, and neighborhoods that step down toward the water in every direction. The waterfront economy sets the wildlife tone: raccoons and rats work the marinas, crab houses, and restaurant blocks, and den in the nearest older buildings.

In the historic streets, bats roost in the tall attics and church rooflines, squirrels work the street canopy, and skunks and opossums den under the raised porches of the frame housing. The newer subdivisions on the town's edges add groundhogs along the field lines and raccoons commuting from the creek bottoms. Dorchester is also marsh country — the Blackwater refuge lands lie just south of town — and the sheer abundance of water, marsh, and farmland around Cambridge means animal pressure on homes is constant rather than seasonal. Cambridge inspections divide cleanly: waterfront and commercial-adjacent homes need the rat-and-raccoon program, in-town homes need rooflines and porches, and edge properties need burrows and outbuildings — and many homes need two of the three.

faqs.q: Animals keep coming up the ditch behind my Hurlock home — how do we stop them?
faqs.a: The tax ditches around Hurlock are permanent travel corridors, so the strategy is not to empty the ditch — it is to make your structures uninteresting and impenetrable. We identify what is actually denning on your lot, usually skunks or opossums under a porch or shed, or a raccoon in the crawlspace, remove those animals, and screen every ground-level opening with buried mesh that digging cannot defeat. Groundhog burrows in the ditch bank get trapped and collapsed where they threaten a foundation or slab. New animals will always pass along the ditch; the goal is that none of them can move in, and that goal is achievable.

faqs.q: Are the snakes around Hurlock farm buildings dangerous?
faqs.a: Almost always they are black rat snakes — long, dark, nonvenomous, and the best rodent control a grain shed can have — though we never ask a homeowner to identify a snake themselves. All Maryland snakes are protected and operators may not kill them; if a snake is inside a home or a building where it cannot stay, we capture it without harm and release it on site at a distance from the house or within two miles, as the law provides. Copperheads favor drier, rockier ground than Hurlock's wet ditch country, but any snake you are unsure of should be left alone until it is identified.

Hurlock.wildlife_intro:
Hurlock is a small farming and food-processing town in northern Dorchester County, set in flat, drained farmland laced with ditches and tax ditches that run for miles. Those ditches are the town's wildlife highways: muskrats work the banks, raccoons and opossums travel the ditch lines, and skunks den where the lines pass behind the town's modest homes.

The housing is mostly small frame and brick homes from the early and mid-1900s, with farmhouses on the roads out of town. Groundhogs dig the ditch banks and field edges and move under sheds and porches from there; bats use the older attics in summer; and black rat snakes patrol the grain storage and chicken houses on the farm properties, where experienced owners value them. Hurlock's animal work is unpretentious and practical — the openings are at ground level more often than at the roofline, the burrows are in the ditch bank behind the house, and the fix is usually a combination of trapping, backfilling, and honest screening of the crawlspace and outbuildings. Properties on the town's edge, where a yard is really the first field, get the full farm treatment in a single visit.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a East New Market chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Dorchester County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

faqs.q: When is wildlife pressure worst in East New Market?
faqs.a: Spring denning and the fall push indoors are the two busy waves in Dorchester County, with bat colonies and mole damage peaking in summer. If you are hearing noise or seeing digging in East New Market, calling at the first sign almost always makes for a simpler, cheaper job.

East New Market.wildlife_intro:
East New Market gives our crew a Dorchester mix shaped by Fishing Bay and the Honga River marshes and the housing around it. Raccoons are the everyday Dorchester call — in Cambridge attics, Hurlock farm outbuildings and waterfront homes that sit between crabbing seasons — with skunks and opossums under the county's many raised houses and sheds, and bats in Cambridge's older stock — and East New Market is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Cambridge keeps Victorian waterfront and worker housing, Hurlock is a rail and farm town, East New Market and Vienna are small historic villages, and much of the county is watermen's homes and farmhouses. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in East New Market; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most East New Market jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Vienna porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Vienna with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Vienna homes?
faqs.a: Yes — older rooflines and quiet attics in Vienna host summer colonies, and in Dorchester County the work is exclusion only, timed around the maternity season. Our crew maps every entry, fits one-way exits in the right window, and seals the building behind the bats.
